sections.content: If you have been searching for an affordable, high-yield real estate market that most investors are still sleeping on, look no further than Dayton, Ohio. With median home prices sitting well below the national average, strong rental demand, and a recovering local economy, the real estate deals in Dayton OH are attracting a growing wave of savvy investors from across the country. Whether you are a first-time buyer or a seasoned wholesaler, this guide will walk you through everything you need to know to profit in this market. If you are brand new to the game, start with our [Real Estate Investing for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) guide before diving in.
Dayton OH Market Overview: Why Investors Are Paying Attention

Dayton is the sixth-largest city in Ohio, home to roughly 140,000 residents in the city proper and over 800,000 in the greater metro area. The city has deep roots in manufacturing and aerospace, anchored by Wright-Patterson Air Force Base — one of the largest Air Force installations in the country and a major economic driver with over 30,000 employees. Dayton is also home to several universities, including the University of Dayton and Wright State University, which creates consistent rental demand from students and faculty alike. The local economy has diversified significantly over the past decade, adding healthcare, logistics, and tech jobs that have stabilized the housing market.
Average Home Prices and What Your Dollar Gets You

As of 2024, the median home price in Dayton sits around $135,000 to $150,000, compared to the national median of roughly $420,000. In many investor-friendly zip codes, you can still find single-family homes priced between $40,000 and $90,000 that rent for $800 to $1,200 per month. That kind of price-to-rent ratio is nearly impossible to find in coastal markets or even in cities like Columbus or Cleveland. Distressed properties and bank-owned homes in Dayton regularly sell for $20,000 to $60,000, making the city a prime hunting ground for wholesalers and fix-and-flip investors. Best Neighborhoods for Real Estate Investors in Dayton

Not every zip code in Dayton is created equal. Knowing where to focus your energy will save you time and money. Here are the neighborhoods and surrounding suburbs that consistently deliver strong returns for investors.
Top Areas for Rentals and Flips

items: Kettering — A stable suburb south of Dayton with median home prices around $150,000–$180,000. Strong owner-occupant demand and low vacancy rates make it ideal for buy-and-hold investors.

Trotwood — One of the most affordable entry points in the metro. Prices often range from $30,000 to $70,000 with decent rental demand. Higher risk, but higher potential returns for seasoned investors.
Huber Heights — A well-established suburb with consistent rental demand, good schools, and median prices around $160,000. Great for long-term landlords.
Riverside — Located near Wright-Patterson AFB, this area sees steady demand from military families, offering low vacancy and stable tenants.
Five Oaks and Westwood — Inner-city neighborhoods with very low acquisition costs. Best for experienced investors comfortable with higher management intensity.
Beavercreek — A higher-end suburb with stronger appreciation potential and access to the Air Force Base workforce. Entry prices are higher but so are rents.
Downtown Dayton — Ongoing revitalization efforts are drawing younger residents and remote workers, creating opportunities in small multifamily and mixed-use properties.

sections.content: Pro Tip: Focus on properties within a 10-minute drive of Wright-Patterson AFB. Military families receive housing allowances, pay on time, and tend to stay for 2–3 year assignments. This dramatically reduces turnover and vacancy costs for landlords.
Types of Real Estate Deals Available in Dayton OH
Wholesale Deals

Dayton is one of the best wholesale markets in the Midwest. The volume of distressed, vacant, and probate properties is high, and motivated sellers are not hard to find. Wholesalers can regularly assign contracts for $5,000 to $20,000 in assignment fees on deals that end buyers can acquire for $40,000 to $80,000. The key is building a strong buyers list and learning to move quickly. Check out our guide on [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) if you want a step-by-step breakdown of how the process works. For deal evaluation, run your numbers through our free [Wholesale Deal Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) before you lock anything up.
Fix and Flip

Fix-and-flip investors are active throughout the Dayton metro, particularly in Kettering, Huber Heights, and Riverside. A typical flip in Dayton might involve buying a property for $55,000, investing $30,000 to $45,000 in renovations, and reselling for $130,000 to $160,000. That leaves room for a $20,000 to $40,000 gross profit before holding costs and agent fees. The key is accurate ARV estimation — do not skip your comparable sales analysis. The market moves at a moderate pace, so you are not racing against a red-hot bidding war, but you do need to price correctly to sell within 30 to 60 days.
Buy-and-Hold Rentals

For landlords chasing cash flow, Dayton is a serious contender. A $90,000 single-family home in Kettering or Huber Heights can rent for $1,000 to $1,200 per month. After a 20% down payment, your mortgage payment would be around $400 to $450 at current rates, leaving strong monthly cash flow even after taxes, insurance, and a management fee. Small multifamily properties — duplexes and triplexes — are also abundant and affordable, with many available in the $80,000 to $130,000 range. These are ideal for investors looking to house-hack or scale a portfolio efficiently.
Dayton Real Estate Market Trends to Watch in 2024 and 2025

Dayton's housing market has been quietly strengthening. Home prices have appreciated roughly 8–12% annually over the past three years, driven by inventory shortages and increased demand from remote workers relocating from more expensive cities. However, prices remain far below national averages, meaning there is still significant room for growth. The city's downtown revitalization — including new apartment complexes, a renovated convention center, and expanding restaurant and retail districts — is attracting younger buyers and renters who are pushing demand in previously overlooked neighborhoods. Additionally, Ohio's landlord-friendly laws make it easier to manage properties here compared to states like California or New York.

"Dayton is the kind of market where you can still buy right, manage right, and build real wealth. The numbers work in ways they just don't in most other cities right now." — Common sentiment among active Midwest real estate investors
Tips for Out-of-State Investors Looking at Dayton OH

Out-of-state investors are increasingly targeting Dayton for its affordability and cash flow, but remote investing comes with its own set of challenges. Here is how to set yourself up for success from a distance.

items: Build a local team first — Find a reliable property manager, a real estate attorney familiar with Ohio law, and a local contractor before you close your first deal. These relationships are everything.

Use data to find off-market deals — Direct mail, driving for dollars (via apps), and targeted online outreach are all effective in Dayton. Learn more in our guide on [How to Find Off-Market Real Estate Deals](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/off-market-real-estate-deals).
Visit before you buy — At least for your first deal, fly in for a day or two. Walking neighborhoods gives you context that no photo or Zillow listing can replicate.
Understand Ohio landlord-tenant law — Ohio is generally landlord-friendly, but you still need to follow proper notice procedures for evictions and security deposit rules.

Run conservative numbers — Plug your deals into a calculator and stress-test them. Assume 10% vacancy, 10% management fee, and a monthly maintenance reserve of $100–$150 per unit. If the deal still works, move forward.
Join local investor groups — The Dayton REIA (Real Estate Investors Association) and local Facebook groups connect you with active buyers, sellers, and wholesalers who know the market inside and out.

Leverage technology to analyze deals faster — Platforms like AIWholesail can help you identify and evaluate deals in the [Dayton market](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dayton-oh) without needing to be on the ground every week.

sections.content: Pro Tip: When analyzing any Dayton deal remotely, always pull comps from the same zip code and within 0.5 miles when possible. Dayton neighborhoods can change dramatically block by block, so using comps from a neighboring zip can give you a wildly inaccurate ARV. Learn more about accurate deal analysis in our guide on [How to Analyze Real Estate Deals Like a Pro](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/how-to-analyze-real-estate-deals).
Is Dayton OH Right for Your Investment Strategy?

Dayton checks a lot of boxes for investors at every experience level. The low entry prices lower your risk and capital requirements. The rental demand is steady thanks to the military base, universities, and growing job market. The deal volume is high enough to keep wholesalers and flippers busy year-round. And the market has not yet been flooded with competition the way that markets like Memphis or Kansas City have been in recent years. If you move now, you are still early enough to build a meaningful portfolio before prices catch up to demand. The question is not really whether Dayton is a good market — it is whether you are ready to act on it.
